subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: In his first winter in Hamburg, Tuan found the Sundays hardest. At home, the whole family gathered for a long lunch, with his grandmother ladling soup and everyone arguing over the last spring roll. Here, he ate cereal alone in the dorm kitchen while the window fogged. Daniel, a Canadian exchange student, walked in on the third Sunday and asked what smelled so good in a photo on Tuan's phone. “That's my grandmother's noodle soup,” Tuan said, and his voice thinned. Daniel grinned. “Teach me.” The following Sunday, five students crowded round two burners, and Tuan ladled the first bowl, closed his eyes for a second and smiled.

qa.q: What did Tuan eat alone in the dorm kitchen?
qa.a: Tuan ate cereal alone in the dorm kitchen.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling when his voice thinned as he spoke of his grandmother's soup?
qa.a: Tuan felt a sudden, quiet homesickness for the family lunches he was missing.

qa.q: What choice by Daniel began a new routine?
qa.a: Daniel asked about the photo and said, “Teach me,” which led to a weekly noodle-soup Sunday with five students.

qa.q: How might Daniel see the first bowl Tuan ladled?
qa.a: Daniel probably sees that the ritual matters to Tuan and may feel happy to have helped, since Tuan closed his eyes and smiled. 🙂

grounding: A young person abroad misses the family's Sunday meal, feels quiet homesickness and creates a small new ritual with others.

subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: Every morning at home, Sudha woke to filter coffee and her mother's humming from the kitchen. In the university hostel, the alarm rang in a corridor of closed doors. By the second month she had stopped eating breakfast, and nobody noticed. On Sunday Farhan, from across the corridor, asked why she looked so flat. “It's not the same,” Sudha said, then went quiet. Farhan didn't argue. The next Saturday, Sudha borrowed a flask, made filter coffee in the hostel kitchen and knocked on four doors, Farhan's first. “Seven o'clock, the terrace,” she said. They sat on the parapet in blankets, holding steel tumblers, not saying much. Sudha hummed the tune she hadn't realised she knew.

qa.q: What did Sudha wake to every morning at home?
qa.a: Sudha woke to filter coffee and her mother's humming from the kitchen.

qa.q: What did Sudha's “It's not the same” show about how Sudha was feeling?
qa.a: Sudha felt a quiet homesickness and missed the mornings at home, and could not say much more.

qa.q: What did Sudha choose to do on Saturday, and why might it help?
qa.a: Sudha made filter coffee and invited four doors to the terrace at seven, creating a small new morning ritual that gives an anchor like the one at home.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt when Sudha knocked on the door?
qa.a: Farhan may have felt glad to see Sudha reach out, since Farhan had noticed the flat mood a week before and did not push.

grounding: A young person in a hostel misses the small daily rituals of home, feels quiet homesickness and creates a new ritual to feel anchored.

subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: Tejas, you asked why I make appam in a rice cooker every Sunday. Jomon's confession: I'm homesick. At home in Thrissur, Sunday means church at seven, then Ammachi's appam and stew, then everyone fighting over the newspaper. Here in the Delhi hostel, Sunday is just a longer Saturday. My first month, I slept till noon and felt empty, and didn't even know why. Then one Sunday I smelled coconut in the canteen and nearly cried. So I bought a small rice cooker, begged Amma for the batter recipe on a voice call, and started making wobbly appams at eight. Now you and two others turn up with plates. It's not home. But it's a Sunday again.

qa.q: What does Jomon make every Sunday?
qa.a: Appam, in a rice cooker.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling during the first month in the hostel?
qa.a: Jomon felt homesick and empty, sleeping till noon on Sundays without knowing why.

qa.q: What did Jomon do to feel anchored again?
qa.a: Created a small new ritual, making appams every Sunday at eight, and let friends join in.

qa.q: What might Sunday appams mean to Tejas and the two others?
qa.a: A warm shared breakfast that may give them their own small weekly anchor in the hostel too.

grounding: A young person in a hostel misses home's small rituals and builds a new weekly one to feel anchored.

subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: October 20: Hansa woke in her Toronto dorm to grey rain and a lab report due. At home in Ahmedabad it was Diwali morning: Ba drawing rangoli, oil lamps on the steps, the smell of mathiya frying. Hansa watched the family video call on mute during class and felt hollow. October 27: she told Gopika, from the same floor, 'I didn't even light a candle.' Gopika admitted she had cried on Onam. November 3: the two of them and their friend Linh made a tiny rangoli from coloured rice on a paper plate, lit battery candles because real flames weren't allowed, and ate shop-bought laddoos. Hansa photographed it for Ba. It wasn't Diwali. But it was something they'd made, and she decided they would do it every year.

qa.q: What did Hansa, Gopika and Linh use to make the rangoli?
qa.a: Coloured rice on a paper plate.

qa.q: What did Hansa feel watching the family call on mute during class?
qa.a: She felt hollow and homesick, missing the Diwali morning rituals at home.

qa.q: What helped Hansa feel more anchored?
qa.a: Sharing the feeling with Gopika and creating a small new ritual together, a rice rangoli and battery candles, that she plans to repeat.

qa.q: How might Gopika relate to Hansa's homesickness?
qa.a: Gopika had cried on Onam, so she understands and is glad to share a new ritual.

grounding: Over two weeks a student abroad misses festival rituals and creates a small new one with friends.

subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: Tejas, before you fly to Germany, sit with your Uma athai for a minute. When I was nineteen, I went to a hostel in Lucknow, far from Madurai. Nobody there drew kolam at dawn. Nobody said 'saapdu', eat, the way Amma did, three times, even when you'd already eaten. For the first month I felt like a kite with a cut string. Then one morning I took chalk and drew a small kolam outside my hostel room door. The warden frowned but let it stay. By the end of the year, three other girls on my floor were drawing their own designs beside mine: a star, a lotus, a Bengali alpana. So when you feel lost there, don't wait for home to come to you. Draw your little kolam.

qa.q: What did young Uma draw outside her hostel room door?
qa.a: A small kolam, in chalk.

qa.q: What did young Uma mean by feeling 'like a kite with a cut string'?
qa.a: She felt homesick and unanchored, missing the daily rituals of home.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped young Uma, and how did it spread?
qa.a: Drawing a kolam at her door each morning; it anchored her, and by the end of the year three other girls were drawing their own designs beside hers.

qa.q: How might the three girls on the floor have felt joining in?
qa.a: They likely felt homesick too, and adding a star, a lotus or an alpana let them bring a piece of their own homes into the hostel.

grounding: An aunt recalls missing home rituals in a hostel and creating a small daily one that anchored her and others.

subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: Diwali morning in Leeds came with grey drizzle and a nine o'clock exam. Saurabh woke at six out of habit. At home, Maa would be drawing the rangoli by now, Papa arguing with the fairy lights, his sister sneaking sweets from the box before prayers. Here there was only the hum of the hostel fridge. He stood in the shared kitchen, homesick in a way that surprised him, and lit a single tea-light on the windowsill. Farida from across the corridor came in for coffee and saw it. "Is it today?" He nodded. She vanished, then came back with her flatmate Ece and a box of dates. "Five minutes before your exam," Farida said. "We'll make it a thing." They stood round the tiny flame, three people and a humming fridge. Ece asked if she could light the next one.

qa.q: What time was Saurabh's exam?
qa.a: His exam was at nine o'clock.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling in the shared kitchen?
qa.a: He felt homesick in a way that surprised him, missing the rangoli, the lights and the sweets at home.

qa.q: Why did the tea-light help Saurabh feel more anchored?
qa.a: It was a small new ritual that kept a piece of home, and sharing it with Farida and Ece turned it into something he belonged to here.

qa.q: How might Farida see the tiny flame on the windowsill?
qa.a: She likely read it as a sign he was missing home, and wanted to make his morning less lonely by joining in.

grounding: Shows a young man abroad missing festival mornings at home and creating a small new ritual with hostel friends.
